clue.text: Einstein retrospectively taking legal action over equation's origin

indicators.note: To look at something retrospectively is to look back over ground already covered, so the word beside it is read from its last letter to its first.
One thing laid over another covers it, so what has just been turned round closes about the single letter named next.

parts.note: to sue somebody is to take legal action against them
the letter equation begins with, its origin

explanation.surface: A physicist being taken to court over where his famous formula came from.
explanation.walkthrough: The name at the front is the definition rather than the wordplay: it stands for the quality, not the man. E=mc² is the equation the surface is pointing at, and only its opening letter is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Einstein is the name English reaches for when it wants an example of a genius, so the definition names the most famous instance rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Lustrous, wingless bug

indicators.note: wingless takes off the wings, the letters at either edge of the word

parts.note: glistening means shining, lustrous

explanation.surface: A naturalist describes a glossy insect that has no wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bug' looks like the insect the surface describes, but it is a verb: to bug a room is to eavesdrop on it.
explanation.definitionFit: To bug is to plant a hidden microphone so as to eavesdrop, which is what listening in means.

clue.text: Parched after cycling in area south of Suez

indicators.note: cycling means the letters go round, so a block from the front of the word moves to the back

parts.note: seared means scorched or dried up, parched

explanation.surface: A traveller describes a parched region south of Suez after a long bicycle ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' reads as riding a bike, but it moves the opening SEA of SEARED round to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Sea is the stretch of water that begins at the Gulf of Suez and runs south between Africa and Arabia.

clue.text: Loose gravel's slippery stuff

indicators.note: Something loose is not fixed in place, and letters that are not fixed in place will not stay in the order the clue prints them.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, the apostrophe counting for nothing

explanation.surface: Loose gravel on a mountain road and the slithery mess it makes underfoot.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe does the hiding: 'gravel's' reads as a possessive introducing the definition, and the S it carries is the seventh letter of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Verglas is the film of clear ice that forms on rock or road, so 'slippery stuff' names it by what makes climbers dread it.

clue.text: See you doffing cap a lot

indicators.note: To doff a cap is to lift it off, and in a down entry the cap of a word is the letter sitting at the top of it.

parts.note: toodles, from toodle-oo, is a breezy British way of saying goodbye

explanation.surface: Somebody raising their hat as they say goodbye.
explanation.walkthrough: The last two words read as part of the farewell — see you a lot — and they are the definition standing alone. Down clues can treat the top letter of a word as its hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Oodles is the informal noun for a great quantity, which is what 'a lot' says when nobody is counting.

clue.text: Fossil fuel left dons suffering agonies

indicators.note: To don a coat is to climb inside it, so the letter doing the donning ends up within the letters it puts on.
Anything suffering is being put through the mill, and letters put through it come out in an order they did not go in.

parts.note: seven letters of fodder
l = left, as stamped inside a pair of boots

explanation.surface: A fuel shortage leaving university dons in agony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' reads as a plural noun, the college teachers the fuel has abandoned, and works as the verb for putting a garment on. Gasoline is what most of the English-speaking world calls petrol.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasoline is refined from crude oil, so it belongs to the fossil-fuel family the definition names rather than being a synonym for one.

clue.text: Edges of empire sacked by Egypt's last queen

indicators.note: sacked means plundered and wrecked, as an empire's capital might be, so its letters are thrown into disorder
last points to the final letter of the country's name, Egypt

parts.note: the name Egypt, its possessive dropped
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword queen

explanation.surface: The outer reaches of an empire are plundered by the last queen of Egypt, Cleopatra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Egypt's last queen' calls up Cleopatra, but it splits into T, the last letter of Egypt, and ER, Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: A perimeter is the outer boundary of an area, so it is made of its edges, though the clue's plural is looser than the answer.

clue.text: Told ally to lose three pounds before tomorrow

indicators.note: to lose says the pound symbols are taken out of the words told ally, wherever they sit

parts.note: the first of the three pound letters, the one in told
L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound; there are three in told ally, one here and two taken first

explanation.surface: Someone tells a friend they need to lose three pounds in weight before tomorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three pounds' looks like a diet target, but it is three Ls: one comes out of TOLD and two out of ALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Today is the day that comes just before tomorrow; the definition describes it by its place in time.

clue.text: Bring this novel for Leo, perhaps

indicators.note: Something novel has not been seen in that shape before, so the letters are wanted in an arrangement the clue has not printed.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Asking somebody to bring a new book along for a friend called Leo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' sits between the fodder and the definition passing as the book in the surface, and 'perhaps' is the standard flag that Leo is one example of the answer rather than a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Leo is one of the twelve signs of the zodiac people are born under, so it defines the answer by being an instance of it.

clue.text: Reportedly failing, fell

indicators.note: A report passes on what somebody said, so the word wanted is reached by ear and then written down some other way.

parts.note: a failing is a flaw, and British speech leaves the r unsounded, so the two words come out identical aloud

explanation.surface: Word reaching you that somebody in decline has gone over.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words read as talk about a person's health, and the last one is the definition: 'fell' here is the verb for knocking a man down, not the past tense of falling.
explanation.definitionFit: To floor somebody is to knock them to the ground, which is what a boxer does when he fells an opponent — verb for verb.

clue.text: Offer and appraisal both turned out to be unwritten

indicators.note: Turned out means facing outwards, so from each of the two words named you keep only the letters standing at its ends.

parts.note: the letters at the two ends of the word, with everything between them gone
the same treatment for the longer word: what it opens with and what it closes on

explanation.surface: A bid and a valuation that were never actually put down on paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out to be' reads as a discovery about a deal and hides an instruction about letters. An oral offer is precisely the kind that leaves nothing on paper, so surface and answer describe one situation.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral agreement is made in speech alone, so 'unwritten' picks the sense of the word that contrasts with paper rather than the one about mouths.

clue.text: Some thoughts on Gabonese Bantu language

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a part of it, so what is wanted is a run of letters taken from inside the words that follow rather than all of them.

parts.note: six letters in a row, beginning inside the first word and finishing inside the last

explanation.surface: A few opinions offered about the languages spoken in Gabon.
explanation.walkthrough: The country is the misdirection: this language belongs to southern Africa, thousands of miles from Gabon, and the letters run straight across the gaps between the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Tsonga is the Bantu language of southern Mozambique and the South African lowveld, so the definition names it by the family it belongs to.

clue.text: Always, come rain or shine, tongue in cheek?

definitions.text: Always, come rain or shine, tongue in cheek?

parts.note: the letter each of these five words begins with, taken in the order printed
the last three words keep the run going, the little joining word included

explanation.surface: Somebody promising to turn up whatever the weather, and not entirely meaning it.
explanation.walkthrough: The sentence performs what it names: read the letter each word starts with and the clue has written the answer out along its own front edge. 'Tongue in cheek' is the setter admitting as much.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrostic is a piece of writing whose initial letters spell something out, and this clue is one, which is what the question mark flags.

clue.text: In bits, heads to America (see below)

indicators.note: A head is the front of a thing, so what each word named here gives up is the letter it starts with and nothing more.

parts.note: the letter the country's name opens with
the first letter of the little cross-reference word inside the bracket
below = under, the preposition at face value

explanation.surface: A line in a guidebook sending you off to America and pointing further down the page.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is doing the hiding: '(see below)' reads as a typesetter's cross-reference, and both words inside it are wordplay. Asunder survives in modern English almost only in 'torn asunder'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in bits has been broken apart, and asunder is the adverb English keeps for exactly that state — put asunder, torn asunder.

clue.text: False promise goads nurses

indicators.note: To nurse a thing is to hold it in your arms, so the word doing the nursing closes round the letters named before it.

parts.note: a rider's spurs are what goad a horse forward
an IOU is a scribbled promise to pay, the letters standing for 'I owe you'

explanation.surface: A pay pledge that turns out to be empty, and the nursing staff it has infuriated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' is the profession the surface is angry on behalf of and a verb underneath, since to nurse something is to cradle it. IOU is worth owning: three letters that spell out what you say when you owe money.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spurious is not what it claims to be, so 'False' is the plain synonym in the counterfeit sense rather than the merely mistaken one.

clue.text: Authentic beach huts oddly disappearing

indicators.note: The odd ones are the first, the third, the fifth and so on, and here they are the ones that go, leaving whatever stands in the even places.

parts.note: run the two words together and keep only what sits in the even positions

explanation.surface: Beach huts vanishing one by one from a seafront.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' is doing arithmetic rather than describing how strange the disappearance is. Echt is German for genuine, borrowed whole into English and used mostly of art and antiques.
explanation.definitionFit: Echt is the German word for real, used in English of the true article as opposed to a copy of it.

clue.text: Earliest of begonias continued blooming

definitions.note: The definition ends in -ing and the answer in -ed, which does not matter here because both are adjectives of exasperation and neither is a live participle: a blasted door is a blooming door.

indicators.note: The earliest part of a word is where it starts, so nothing but the opening letter of the flower named next is taken.

parts.note: the letter begonias opens with
a downpour that continued lasted

explanation.surface: The first begonias of the season carrying on flowering.
explanation.walkthrough: Definition and answer are both mild British swearing dressed up as gardening. Nothing in the clue is really about flowers: the begonias are there for their first letter and for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are polite stand-ins for a curse — a blasted nuisance, a blooming nuisance — so the fit is the exasperated sense, not the floral one.

clue.text: Buys barrier to stop litter droppers

indicators.note: To stop a gap is to plug it, so the barrier is packed into the middle of the other word instead of standing beside it.

parts.note: a sow drops a litter of piglets
a wall is the plainest barrier there is

explanation.surface: Buying a fence to keep people from dumping rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter droppers' is people tossing crisp packets about in the surface and pigs in the wordplay. 'Buys' is the sense in 'I don't buy it' — accepting a story rather than paying for anything.
explanation.definitionFit: To swallow a story is to accept it whole, which is exactly the sense of 'buys' in 'I'm not buying that'.

clue.text: Familiar with your sib's butt trouble

parts.note: pert means forward and cheeky, familiar in the way that annoys people
the way the word gets typed on a phone by somebody in a hurry

indicators.note: The butt of a thing is its blunt back end, so what is taken from the word in front is the letter it finishes on.

parts.note: the end of sib, the short form of sibling

explanation.surface: Knowing rather too much about your brother's or sister's backside complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: The lavatorial surface is a decoy: 'butt' is not the body part but the blunt end of a word, and text-message spelling is fair game for a Guardian setter.
explanation.definitionFit: To perturb somebody is to trouble them, in the sense of unsettling a person's mind rather than putting them to any inconvenience.

clue.text: Free money for Americans, with short notice

parts.note: a buck is a dollar
to take notice of something is to heed it, and this heed stops a letter early

explanation.surface: Cash handed to Americans at very short notice.
explanation.walkthrough: Buckshee is army slang out of the Persian baksheesh, a tip or a handout, and it settled into British English meaning got for nothing. The surface never leaves the world of money.
explanation.definitionFit: Buckshee means had for nothing, so 'Free' is being used in the costing-nothing sense rather than the one about liberty.

clue.text: Roger backing strike for change in Russia

indicators.note: Backing a thing is getting behind it, and a word read from behind hands over its letters in the opposite order.

parts.note: 'Roger' on the radio means message received, which is to say OK
a bird's peck is a short sharp strike with the beak

explanation.surface: Roger throwing his support behind a strike for reform in Russia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roger' opens the clue looking like a man's name and is radio code for 'received'. A kopeck is a hundredth of a rouble, so it really is Russian small change.
explanation.definitionFit: A kopeck is the hundredth part of a rouble, so the definition means coinage of small value rather than anything that alters.

clue.text: Goes off round centre of Damascus and swelters

indicators.note: round says the decay word wraps itself around the middle of the city's name

parts.note: food that goes off rots

indicators.note: the centre of an eight-letter word is its middle two letters

parts.note: its middle two letters are taken

explanation.surface: A traveller in Damascus finds the food spoiling as the city centre swelters in the heat.
explanation.walkthrough: Damascus has an even number of letters, so its 'centre' is two letters, not one.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast is informally to be uncomfortably hot, so someone who roasts swelters in the heat.

clue.text: Lacking vigour in harem is shameful

indicators.note: What is in something sits inside it, so the letters wanted are already sitting inside the words that come after it.

parts.note: six letters in a row that start partway through one word and run on across the joins

explanation.surface: Feebleness in a harem being held up as a disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: The run crosses two word joins, which is what keeps it out of sight, and 'in' is the only word telling you to look — it reads as an ordinary preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: Remiss means slack, and the word covers a want of energy quite as much as neglect of a duty.

clue.text: Chasing game, regularly dispatching zebras and big cats

parts.note: tig is the British playground game of chase, called tag in most other places

indicators.note: Dispatching is killing off, and doing it regularly means at every other letter, so the ones in the odd places never arrive.

parts.note: what is left of the word once the odd-numbered letters have gone

explanation.surface: Hunters chasing game across the plains and picking off zebras as they go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chasing game' reads as the pursuit of prey, which is what the definition's animals do all day, and it is the name of a children's game. Zebras and big cats sit in one picture, so the join never shows.
explanation.definitionFit: Tigers are the largest of the big cats, so the definition names the group they belong to — plural for plural.

clue.text: Delicate international agent put on weight

indicators.note: Something put on a thing lands on top of it, so the pieces named before this phrase follow the letter named after it.

parts.note: w = weight, the standard abbreviation on any chart
i = international, the usual short form in sport and politics
an agent in the espionage sense is a spy

explanation.surface: A frail secret agent who has been eating rather too well.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the contradiction: putting on weight is the last thing anyone delicate does. In an across clue a piece put 'on' another follows it, which is why the weight comes first of all.
explanation.definitionFit: Wispy describes something thin and insubstantial — a wispy beard, a wispy cloud — so 'Delicate' means fineness here rather than fragility.

clue.text: Exciting yet gloomy study of roots

indicators.note: To excite something is to stir it up, and letters stirred up do not settle back into the order they were given in.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A book about plant roots that manages to be gripping and depressing at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roots' is the word-origin kind rather than the garden kind, and 'Exciting' opens the clue as an adjective while doing a verb's work on the two words beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Etymology is the study of where words come from — their roots — so the definition uses 'roots' in the linguistic sense the surface keeps hidden.

clue.text: Brief question for bachelor in automobile

indicators.note: for means in place of, so the question letters take over from the bachelor letter
in says the exchange happens within the name of the car, where the bachelor letter is found

parts.note: a Buick is an American make of car
B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in degree titles
Q is a standard abbreviation for question, as in Q and A

explanation.surface: A short question for an unmarried man sitting in a car.
explanation.walkthrough: Buick is a General Motors car brand, so the 'automobile' is BUICK, and 'question for bachelor' swaps its B for Q.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick visit is a short one, so the adjective quick means brief, lasting little time.

clue.text: Oblique signal in setter's work

parts.note: cross means lying athwart something, as in a crosswind or a cross-beam
the word is the signal to go, as in 'just say the word'

explanation.surface: A sideways hint slipped into the puzzle-maker's own handiwork.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is the person who writes the puzzle, not a dog and not somebody laying a table. This being the Guardian's 30,000th, the final across answer names the thing you are holding.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword is what a setter produces, so the definition points at the answer through the job of the person who makes it.
